## From last time

**Smith-Waterman** finds the best **local** alignment:
The best match between *part* of one sequence and *part* of another.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 180%;"}
```{.my-blue-code}
TTTTACGTCA
    ||||||
    ACGTCAGGGG
```
:::

. . .

"Is some region of this database sequence similar to some region of my
sequence?" is a **local** alignment question.

That is the question you ask every time you run BLAST.

::: {.notes}
0:00-1:00

Anchor in the end of last lecture. The point to land: BLAST is a local
alignment search, so everything today builds on Smith-Waterman.
:::

## When you use BLAST

::: {.incremental}
-   Paste in a sequence and click a button
-   A few seconds later: A ranked list of similar sequences
-   Searched against GenBank: About **60 trillion** bases^[GenBank release 273.0,
    August 2026: $6 \times 10^{13}$ bases]
:::

. . .

***How is that possible?!***

::: {.notes}
1:00-1:45

Ask for a show of hands: who has used BLAST? Most will have. Ask them to
guess how it works before moving on.
:::

## Can we just use Smith-Waterman?

The scoring table has $m \times n$ cells ($O(mn)$).

. . .

One 150-base read against GenBank:

$$
150 \times (6 \times 10^{13}) \approx 9 \times 10^{15} \text{ cells}
$$

::: {.incremental style="font-size: 80%;"}
-   Optimized code, a billion cells per second: **Over 3 months**
-   Our Python code: **A century or more** (you will measure this today)
-   One sequencing run has **billions** of reads
    -   Click, go on summer vacation, repeat
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
A faster computer does not fix this. We need to avoid doing most of the work.
:::

::: {.notes}
1:45-3:30

9e15 cells at 1e9 cells/s is ~104 days. Our pure-Python aligner runs at
roughly 2-3 million cells/s, which works out to ~100-150 years; they will get
their own number in Part 2 of the notebook.

Callback to the complexity lecture: this is the "buying a cluster does not
fix it" point.
:::

## Heuristic algorithms

From our algorithms lecture:

::: {style="font-size: 80%;"}
-   Smith-Waterman is optimal but far too slow to scan all of GenBank
-   BLAST first finds short exact seed matches, then only extends around those
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
"Approximate answer today" beats "exact answer in nine years."
:::

. . .

Today we unpack that second bullet: **BLAST**^[@blast], the
**B**asic **L**ocal **A**lignment **S**earch **T**ool.

::: {.notes}
3:30-4:15

This is verbatim from the Topic 4 heuristics slide. The 1990 BLAST paper is
among the most cited papers in all of science.
:::

# Seed and extend {background-color="#1b3a5c"}

## The key insight

Two homologous sequences almost always share at least one **short, exact**
match.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 180%;"}
```{.my-blue-code}
TGCTTACCAGTCAGGT
TGCTTACGAGTCATTG
```
:::

. . .

So:

::: {.incremental}
1.  Find short exact matches (**seeds**) &mdash; fast!
2.  Do alignment work **only** near the seeds
3.  Ignore the rest of the database
:::

::: {.notes}
4:15-5:15

Let them spot the shared runs: TGCTTAC at the start and AGTCA in the middle.
Finding exact matches is a problem we already know how to solve very fast.
:::

## Step 0: Index the database, once

Finding exact matches of length $k$ fast?

-   We have done this!

. . .

The **$k$-mer dictionary** from our string search lecture:

```python
{"TGCT": [7], "GCTT": [8], "CTTA": [9], ...}
```

::: {.incremental}
-   Build it **once** for the whole database
-   Every lookup after that is $O(1)$
-   NCBI builds its BLAST databases long before you submit a query
:::

::: {.notes}
5:15-6:15

Direct callback to the string search timing result: the setup cost gets
spread over an enormous number of searches. Real BLAST builds a lookup table
of query words and scans the database, but the idea (index so that exact
matches are instant) is the same. Don't go into that distinction.
:::

## Step 1: Seeds

Look up every $k$-mer of the query ($k = 4$ below):

::: {style="font-size: 110%;"}
```
query:   TGCTTACCAGTCAGGT
subject: GGATCCATGCTTACGAGTCATTGCAACGT
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 75%;"}
| Query $k$-mer | Query position | Subject position(s) |
|:-:|--:|--:|
| `TGCT` | 0 | 7 |
| `GCTT` | 1 | 8 |
| `CTTA` | 2 | 9 |
| `TTAC` | 3 | 10 |
| `TACC` | 4 | &mdash; |
| &hellip; | | |
| `AGTC` | 8 | 15 |
| `GTCA` | 9 | 16 |
:::

::: {.notes}
6:15-7:15

Each hit is a seed: a (query position, subject position) pair. This is
exactly the find_seeds function they will write (Challenge 4). The same
example is in the notebook.
:::

## Homologous seeds often line up on diagonals

::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}
| Seed | Query pos | Subject pos | Subject $-$ query |
|:-:|--:|--:|--:|
| `TGCT` | 0 | 7 | **7** |
| `GCTT` | 1 | 8 | **7** |
| `CTTA` | 2 | 9 | **7** |
| `TTAC` | 3 | 10 | **7** |
| `AGTC` | 8 | 15 | **7** |
| `GTCA` | 9 | 16 | **7** |
:::

. . .

All six are on the same **diagonal** of a dotplot: Pieces of the same
alignment!

. . .

A seed alone on its own diagonal is usually just **chance**.

::: {.notes}
7:15-8:15

Tie to the dotplots from the alignment exercise: homology shows up as
diagonal runs, and isolated dots are noise. In the notebook, they will see
seeds from a real read pile up on two diagonals separated by a 6-base
deletion.
:::

## Step 2: Extend without gaps

Grow the seed one base at a time, keeping a **running score**
(match $+1$, mismatch $-1$):

::: {style="font-size: 55%;"}
| | seed | | | | | | | | | | | | |
|:--|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| **query**   | TGCT | T | A | C | C | A | G | T | C | A | G | G | T |
| **subject** | TGCT | T | A | C | G | A | G | T | C | A | T | T | G |
| **score** | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 | 10 | [**11**]{style="color: #0057B8;"} | 10 | 9 | 8 |
:::

. . .

**X-drop rule**: stop once the score falls more than $X$ below the best score
seen (here $X = 2$), then trim back to the best.

. . .

The result is a **high-scoring segment pair** (HSP) with a score of 11.

::: {.notes}
8:15-10:00

Walk through the running score. The mismatch at the 8th column costs a point,
but the matches after it recover. Once we run off the end of the homologous
region, the score falls steadily, and X-drop stops us from wasting time.
BLAST (and extend_seed in the notebook) also extends to the left; same idea.
:::

## Indels break ungapped extension

::: {style="font-size: 170%;"}
```{.my-blue-code}
Alpha: CCATGCTAT------CTCTGGGA
Wuhan: CCATGCTATACATGTCTCTGGGA
```
:::


::: {.incremental}
-   Seeds on both sides of the indel, but on **two different diagonals**
-   Ungapped extension gives two separate HSPs
:::

. . .

**Gapped BLAST**^[@gappedblast]: Run a gapped alignment, but only in the short
region around a good HSP.

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Run the Smith-Waterman aligner on ~200 bases, ***NOT*** 60 trillion.
:::

::: {.notes}
10:00-11:15

This is the spike 69-70 deletion they aligned last time (Alpha vs. Wuhan). In
the notebook, simple_blast runs their own align_local on a small window around
the best HSP. Real gapped BLAST uses an X-drop version of dynamic
programming rather than a fixed window; our window is a simplification.
:::

## Step 3: Is the hit meaningful?

::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}
In a database of 60 trillion bases, many matches happen **by chance**.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}
BLAST reports an **E-value**^[@Altschul1990]: The number of hits scoring at
least this well that you would *expect* by chance in a database this big.

$$
E = K\,m\,n\,e^{-\lambda S}
$$
:::

::: {.incremental style="font-size: 85%;"}
-   Bigger query ($m$) or database ($n$): More chance hits
-   Higher score ($S$): **Exponentially** fewer chance hits
-   $E = 10^{-50}$: Essentially impossible by chance; $E = 5$: Probably just chance
:::

::: {.notes}
11:15-12:45

Keep this light. K and lambda depend on the scoring scheme; no need to say
more. This is a preview of the probability models coming in the next unit.
The notebook reports raw scores only.
:::

# The price of speed {background-color="#1b3a5c"}

## Missing homologous sequences

BLAST only looks where it finds a seed.

. . .

A homolog with **no exact match of $k$ consecutive bases** is invisible to BLAST, no matter
how good the full alignment would be.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 180%;"}
```{.my-blue-code}
TGCTTACCAGTCAGGT
| || ||| || || |
TCCTAACCTGTAAGCT
```
:::

. . .

11 of 16 bases identical, but never more than 3 in a row

-   With $k = 4$, we miss it!

::: {.notes}
12:45-13:45

The two sequences are 69% identical (11 of 16 positions), which is clearly
similar, but the longest identical run is 3 bases. Point: sensitivity depends
on the word size, not just on how similar the sequences are.
:::

## The word size ($k$) trade-off

Number of chance seeds for a 150-base query against GenBank
($\approx m\,n / 4^k$):

::: {style="font-size: 90%;"}
| Word size $k$ | Chance seeds | Needs an exact run of |
|--:|--:|--:|
| 7 | $\sim 5 \times 10^{11}$ | 7 bases |
| 11 | $\sim 2 \times 10^{9}$ | 11 bases |
| 28 | $\sim 0.1$ | 28 bases |
:::

. . .

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Small $k$**

More sensitive, much slower
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Large $k$**

Much faster, misses divergent homologs
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
13:45-15:15

Each base shorter makes a chance match 4 times more likely. Every chance seed
has to be extended and thrown away. In the notebook, they will see k = 7
produce over a thousand chance seeds against a single 30 kb genome, and a
~100-200x slowdown relative to k = 11.
:::

## NCBI's tool choices

::: {style="font-size: 90%;"}
| Program (task) | Word size | Designed for |
|:--|--:|:--|
| `megablast` (default) | 28 | Highly similar sequences |
| `blastn` | 11 | Somewhat similar sequences |
| `blastn-short` | 7 | Short queries (*e.g.*, primers) |
| Protein BLAST | 3 | Proteins (20-letter alphabet) |
:::

. . .

When you pick an option on the BLAST web page, you are choosing a point along
the speed/sensitivity trade-off continuum!

::: {.notes}
15:15-16:15

Protein words can be short because the alphabet is 20 letters (8,000 possible
3-mers), and protein BLAST also accepts similar, not just identical, words.
One sentence on that at most.
:::

## Applying what we learned

Which BLAST program would you use?

::: {.incremental}
-   Which species did this 16S sequence from a soil sample come from?
-   Does a human genome contain a homolog of this frog gene?
-   Where does this 20-base PCR primer bind in the human genome?
:::

::: {.notes}
16:15-17:30

- 16S species ID: megablast (looking for a near-identical match)
- Human homolog of a frog gene: blastn, or better yet protein BLAST, since
  protein sequences change more slowly than DNA
- 20-base primer: blastn-short (a word of 28 cannot fit in the query!)
:::

## BLAST does a bit more

::: {.incremental}
-   Searches **both strands** of DNA
-   Masks **low-complexity** sequences (*e.g.*, `ATATATATAT`) that would seed
    everywhere
-   Protein BLAST requires **two seeds** near each other before extending
-   Reports multiple HSPs per database sequence
:::

. . .

But the core is what you will build today: **Seed, extend, evaluate**

::: {.notes}
17:30-18:15

Low-complexity masking and the two-hit method are both ways of cutting down
on chance seeds, which ties back to the word size slide. In the notebook,
"evaluate" is just a raw-score cutoff (min_score), not an E-value. The stretch goal in
the notebook is about searching both strands.
:::

## Summary

::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}
::: {.incremental}
-   Optimal local alignment is $O(mn)$, but $n$ is **tens of trillions**!
-   **Seed**: Find short exact matches with an index built once
-   **Extend**: Ungapped with the X-drop rule, then gapped only near good HSPs
-   **Evaluate**: E-values suggest whether a hit is better than chance
-   **Word size** sets the speed/sensitivity trade-off
-   BLAST gives up the guarantee of optimality to get an answer fast
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
18:15-19:00

If short on time, cut to the last two bullets.
:::
